topicsPresent: Founding of Kyiv and Rurik dynasty
Volodymyr the Great — Baptism of Rus (988)
Yaroslav the Wise — law and diplomacy
Kyiv as political and religious center
kievan-rus.framingNotes: Uses 'Rus-Ukraine' terminology establishing direct national continuity with modern Ukraine. Embeds explicit Hrushevsky citation (1904) arguing Ukrainian — not Russian — succession to Kievan Rus. Written 2024, post-full-scale invasion. Contemporary political stakes visible throughout.
kievan-rus.analystNotes: Kievan Rus is this curriculum's origin story. Maximum coverage among all corpus sources for this region.

topicsPresent: Rurik dynasty as origin of Russian statehood
Oleg capturing Kyiv — 'mother of Russian cities'
Yaroslav the Wise — Russkaya Pravda legal code
kievan-rus.framingNotes: Kyiv described as 'mother of Russian cities' — Russian succession claim made explicit. Rurik portrayed as founder of Russian statehood. No mention of Ukrainian historiographical counter-argument. Same historical entity as Ukrainian textbook, opposite national claim.
kievan-rus.analystNotes: Both textbooks were in classrooms simultaneously in 2024–2025. The competing succession claims are not acknowledged in either.

topicsPresent: Payment of tribute to Golden Horde
mongol-empire.framingNotes: Mongols described as 'поневолювачі' (enslavers). Invasion framed entirely from Rus victim perspective. Mongol Empire as a political or cultural entity — absent.
mongol-empire.analystNotes: 8 pages, all framed as external threat to the curriculum's home polity.

topicsPresent: Mongol state formation under Chinggis Khan
mongol-empire.framingNotes: Significantly more internal Mongol history than Ukrainian textbook. Includes state formation and legal code. However every section is organized around its consequences for Rus. Trade restoration noted in one sentence. Mongol internal civilization subordinated to Russian national trauma narrative.
mongol-empire.analystNotes: Deeper coverage than Ukraine but still instrumentalized. The Mongol Empire as a historical subject in its own right is absent even here.

topicsPresent: Muhammad Tughluq's planned offensive against Transoxiana
mongol-empire.framingNotes: Mongols appear only as military threat to Delhi Sultanate. Chapter keyword list includes 'Mongols' but no section devoted to the Mongol Empire as a subject.
mongol-empire.analystNotes: Third national curriculum, third continent — same structural pattern. Mongol Empire = external threat to the curriculum's home polity.

topicsPresent: Raziyya Sultan — gender and political authority
delhi-sultanate.framingNotes: Richest coverage of any entry in corpus. Notable for including gender (Raziyya), explicit source criticism (tawarikh as court literature), and administrative complexity. Delhi Sultanate is the curriculum's home polity.
delhi-sultanate.analystNotes: Confirms the pattern from the other direction: home polity receives complex, multi-dimensional coverage. Compare with 2-page treatment of Mongols in the same textbook.

mapungubwe.framingNotes: Coverage exists but framed through providential Christian lens. African kingdoms positioned as societies awaiting European missionary contact. Trade and material culture acknowledged; political agency and internal social history limited.
mapungubwe.analystNotes: Only corpus source to cover Mapungubwe. 3 pages in one South African Christian curriculum textbook. Zero coverage in all other corpus sources.
